## ToolPool.kt { #toolpool-kt }

The tool pool: a local library, shared across projects, of tools written in box Kotlin, with their tests and the evidence those tests produced.

[`BoxToolTest`](workspace.md#toolpool-kt-boxtooltest) attaches an executable example to a [`Box.aiTool`](machine-learning.md#boxaitools-kt--aitool) definition, and [`ToolDiagnostics`](workspace.md#toolpool-kt-tooldiagnostics)
keeps bounded per-call evidence ([`ToolCallEvidence`](workspace.md#toolpool-kt-toolcallevidence)) and suite results ([`ToolTestEvidence`](workspace.md#toolpool-kt-tooltestevidence)) keyed
by source hash, so an edited tool does not inherit an old pass. [`ToolPool`](workspace.md#toolpool-kt-toolpool) stores immutable
[`ToolPoolEntry`](workspace.md#toolpool-kt-toolpoolentry) snapshots under `~/.afield/tool-pool`; loading an entry returns its source and
never runs it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/tools/ToolPool.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/ToolPool/)

### ToolDiagnostics { #toolpool-kt-tooldiagnostics }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">ToolDiagnostics</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">tool</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">BoxTool</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/ToolPool/#L85)

Diagnostics attached to a registered tool, rather than a second execution engine. Every entry point uses the same recorder. Records live with the document and survive reopening. Capture is bounded and best effort: a full disk must not turn a successful edit into a reported failure.

### ToolPool { #toolpool-kt-toolpool }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ToolPool</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">directory</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">File</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">File</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">System</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">getProperty</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">&quot;user.home&quot;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="s">&quot;.afield/tool-pool&quot;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/ToolPool/#L179)

A local, cross-project library of box-authored tools. This stores source; it is not a tool registry. Curating is explicit. Loading an entry never runs it or imports the originating project's state. Run the returned source in a normal provider box to register its tools, then test in that project. Keep project-specific dependencies explicit in the provider source and entry description.

## BoxOutputLog.kt { #boxoutputlog-kt }

A bounded server-side record of each box's printed text, errors, `display(...)` channels and
execution verdicts, readable without a websocket.

Readers take [`BoxOutputLog.mark`](workspace.md#boxoutputlog-kt--boxoutputlog--mark) before acting and read [`BoxOutputLog.since`](workspace.md#boxoutputlog-kt--boxoutputlog--since) afterwards to see
what one run produced. The bounds and the feed points are described on [`BoxOutputLog`](workspace.md#boxoutputlog-kt-boxoutputlog).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/diagnostics/BoxOutputLog.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/diagnostics/BoxOutputLog/)

## CodeUseTelemetryService.kt { #codeusetelemetryservice-kt }

The local history of code Field compiles and runs, stored in SQLite and summarised for the
code-use panels and agent tools.

[`CodeUseTelemetryService`](workspace.md#codeusetelemetryservice-kt-codeusetelemetryservice) takes records from the compile, evaluation and launch hooks without
blocking them, persists the source by content hash, and resolves which library symbols each
snippet used. The `CodeUse...Row` and [`CodeUseSummary`](workspace.md#codeusetelemetryservice-kt-codeusesummary) types are the shapes its queries return.
Storage, the analyzers and the failure policy are described on [`CodeUseTelemetryService`](workspace.md#codeusetelemetryservice-kt-codeusetelemetryservice).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/diagnostics/CodeUseTelemetryService.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/diagnostics/CodeUseTelemetryService/)

| <a id="codeusetelemetryservice-kt--codeusetelemetryservice--summarysnapshot"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">summarySnapshot</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">CodeUseSummary</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/app/diagnostics/CodeUseTelemetryService/#L589) | Non-blocking counterpart to [`summary`](workspace.md#codeusetelemetryservice-kt--codeusetelemetryservice--summary) for hot polling paths such as the welcome screen. Returns the most recent computed summary immediately (even if a little stale), or a cheap "still gathering" placeholder if none has been computed yet, and kicks off a background recompute when the cache is stale. It never runs the full-table SQLite scans on the caller's thread, so it can't stall Netty request or workspace-search dispatcher threads — the cold first computeSummary() (which can take many seconds on a large database) no longer blocks the welcome response or, by dispatcher starvation, a document the user clicks right after. |

## CoroutineProfiling.kt { #coroutineprofiling-kt }

Per-box coroutine profiling behind the Profiling panel: wall time, CPU time and allocation
charged to the box and strand that launched each continuation.

[`ProfileOrigin`](workspace.md#coroutineprofiling-kt-profileorigin) is the coroutine context element that names the launching box, and
[`CoroutineProfiles`](workspace.md#coroutineprofiling-kt-coroutineprofiles) holds the one capture a process records at a time.
[`installCoroutineProfilingHandlers`](workspace.md#coroutineprofiling-kt--installcoroutineprofilinghandlers) installs the panel's request handlers.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/diagnostics/CoroutineProfiling.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/diagnostics/CoroutineProfiling/)

**Used in:** [Profiling](../profiling_timeline.md)

### CoroutineProfiles { #coroutineprofiling-kt-coroutineprofiles }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">CoroutineProfiles</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/app/diagnostics/CoroutineProfiling/#L96)

Box-owned continuation instrumentation, shared by Runloop and SimulationClock. A continuation's CPU/heap counters exclude its suspended lifetime. No timers or allocations on the disabled dispatch path. Export copies happen on request, not per resume. A process permits one capture at a time; document isolation also applies to stop/snapshot.

## FrameProfile.kt { #frameprofile-kt }

Explicit frame boundaries and named stages for the Profiling panel, for code that has its own
frame loop.

Call [`FrameProfile.beginFrame`](workspace.md#frameprofile-kt--frameprofile--beginframe) once per frame while the panel is recording, and wrap stages in
[`FrameProfile.measure`](workspace.md#frameprofile-kt--frameprofile--measure) or [`profileScope`](workspace.md#frameprofile-kt--profilescope). Nothing is read or allocated while recording is off.

Explicit frame boundaries for the existing Profiling panel. This object does not start a capture. Press Record in the panel, then call [`beginFrame`](workspace.md#frameprofile-kt--frameprofile--beginframe) once per application frame, on a stable thread. Intervals include time between boxes and waits; CPU/heap counters cover that thread only. Use [`measure`](workspace.md#frameprofile-kt--frameprofile--measure) for named inclusive stages. No counter reads or sample allocation while recording is off.

## LatencySpans.kt { #latencyspans-kt }

Where a Field server's own time goes during the moments someone is waiting on it.

Each phase worth attributing is wrapped in [`LatencySpans.time`](workspace.md#latencyspans-kt--latencyspans--time) (creating and bootstrapping a
box's Kotlin engine, compiling a snippet, compiling a shader, building or updating a pipeline,
running a transcript operation) and lands in a ring buffer with its name, the box it belongs to,
the thread it ran on, and a start time in epoch microseconds.
`GET /api/perf/spans?since=<seq>` serves everything recorded after a sequence number.

`tools/feel_bench.py` is what reads it: it measures a step from the client side, then asks the
server which of its own phases that wall time was spent in, and the shared epoch clock is what
lets the two be laid against each other. Recording is always on, because a span costs one
`nanoTime` pair and one array write against work that costs milliseconds.

## JdiProbeHelper.kt { #jdiprobehelper-kt }

The JDI probe helper: a separate JVM that attaches to Field over JDWP and samples a variable at

which installs breakpoints that suspend only the hitting thread and writes responses to stdout.

## RuntimeDebugProbeService.kt { #runtimedebugprobeservice-kt }

The runtime debug probe: samples a symbol at a line of a running box or a `src/` file and shows
the values in the box's "debug probe" output channel.

[`RuntimeDebugProbeService.startProbe`](workspace.md#runtimedebugprobeservice-kt--runtimedebugprobeservice--startprobe) targets box code and
[`RuntimeDebugProbeService.startSourceProbe`](workspace.md#runtimedebugprobeservice-kt--runtimedebugprobeservice--startsourceprobe) targets a source file. Both need Field to have been
launched with a JDWP port; [`RuntimeDebugProbeService.availabilityError`](workspace.md#runtimedebugprobeservice-kt--runtimedebugprobeservice--availabilityerror) explains when it was not.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/diagnostics/debug/RuntimeDebugProbeService.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/diagnostics/debug/RuntimeDebugProbeService/)

## RuntimeProbeProtocol.kt { #runtimeprobeprotocol-kt }

The JSON line protocol between Field and the JDI probe helper process: probe requests and the
ack, sample, error and completion responses.

[`ProbeJson`](workspace.md#runtimeprobeprotocol-kt--probejson) is the codec both sides use; responses are discriminated by their `type` field.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/diagnostics/debug/RuntimeProbeProtocol.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/diagnostics/debug/RuntimeProbeProtocol/)

## PinnedConsole.kt { #pinnedconsole-kt }

A [`LogSink`](machine-learning.md#logging-kt-logsink) that pins chosen channels to a small, non-scrolling region at the *top* of the
terminal while every other log line scrolls normally below it.

The heavy lifting is a single ANSI scroll-region (DECSTBM): the top N rows are fenced off so
ordinary output can only scroll in the region beneath them, which means a plain `println` "just
works" — there is no per-frame render loop over application state. The header is repainted only
when a pinned value actually changes (coalesced by a single daemon tick), and the terminal size
is re-checked about once a second.

Selection is by channel tag: a log event whose comma-separated `channel` contains a pinned tag
(e.g. pinning `"audio"` matches `"info,audio"`) updates that tag's row instead of scrolling.
Configure via the `AFIELD_PIN_CHANNELS` env var (comma/space separated) and/or at runtime with
[`pin`](workspace.md#pinnedconsole-kt--pinnedconsole--pin)/[`unpin`](workspace.md#pinnedconsole-kt--pinnedconsole--unpin)/[`clear`](workspace.md#pinnedconsole-kt--pinnedconsole--clear).

Degrades cleanly: if stdout is not an interactive TTY, ANSI/cursor control is unavailable, or the
terminal is a legacy Windows console (Mordant reports `AnsiLevel.NONE`), pinning switches off and
every event — pinned or not — simply scrolls, with would-be-pinned lines tagged `pin` so they
stay visible. Set `AFIELD_PIN_DISABLE=1` to force this fallback.

Known limitation: raw `System.out.println`/stderr writes elsewhere in the app bypass this sink's
lock and can, very occasionally, interleave with a header repaint. They still scroll below the
header; the visual glitch is transient. Routing all app output through the dispatcher avoids it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/diagnostics/logging/PinnedConsole.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/diagnostics/logging/PinnedConsole/)

## SaveReloadLog.kt { #savereloadlog-kt }

A timestamped append-only log of document save and reload events, written to
`~/.afield/logs/save_reload.log`.

Each line is an ISO instant, the event name in brackets and a message. `logTiming` adds the
elapsed milliseconds since a `System.nanoTime()` start and skips events faster than its threshold.
The file rolls over to `save_reload.log.1` once it reaches 50 MB. Every line also goes to
[`LogDispatcher`](machine-learning.md#logging-kt-logdispatcher) on `info,persist,savereload`, so the log widget and other sinks see it; the
console mutes `info,persist` by default.

## SessionErrorLog.kt { #sessionerrorlog-kt }

A per-session copy of everything written to `System.err`, kept under `build/logs/` in the working
directory, with stack traces also pinned on the console.

[`SessionErrorLog.install`](workspace.md#sessionerrorlog-kt--sessionerrorlog--install) tees stderr: every byte still reaches the real stream, every line is
appended to a `session-<timestamp>-pid<pid>.log` file (the newest 20 are kept, each capped at
32 MB), and a stack trace or slf4j `ERROR` line is raised as a sticky panel that a repaint of the
log viewport does not clear.

Heatmap colouring for the numeric values in the pinned console's rolling stat lines.

[`StatsHeatmap`](workspace.md#statsheatmap-kt-statsheatmap) splits a line such as `fps=61.2 upload=3.4MB` into fragments and colours each
number by how it moved since the last value of the same key on that channel.

## logger.kt { #logger-kt }

The `lprintln` / `lprint` / `lblock` logging calls, which send a message to the server log on a
named channel such as `"info,startup"`.

Each call goes to `LogDispatcher` with the current thread's indent. `lblock` logs a begin line,
runs its block with the indent deepened, and logs a matching end line even if the block throws, so
nested blocks read as a tree. The single-argument forms are deprecated and log on `info,legacy`.
[`formatMillis`](workspace.md#logger-kt--formatmillis) formats a nanosecond duration with its unit for stat lines.

## stdlib_diagnostics.kt { #stdlib-diagnostics-kt }

The frame-presentation log: per-frame graphics timing, written to a file while it runs.

[`frameLogStart`](workspace.md#stdlib-diagnostics-kt--framelogstart) begins recording and returns the path, choosing one if you do not give it one,
and the log keeps growing until [`frameLogStop`](workspace.md#stdlib-diagnostics-kt--framelogstop) closes it. [`frameLogMark`](workspace.md#stdlib-diagnostics-kt--framelogmark) drops a named marker
tied to a frame boundary, so an event can be lined up against the frame that was slow, and
[`frameLogLine`](workspace.md#stdlib-diagnostics-kt--framelogline) appends free text with no frame attached. The `waitAfterPresent` argument changes
what is measured rather than how it is reported: each frame waits for the present to complete,
which gives true per-frame numbers at some cost to throughput.

One of the `stdlib` files, which the `intro` preamble star-imports into every box, so everything
here can be called unqualified, with `Box` as the implicit receiver.

## ButtonControlHandler.kt { #buttoncontrolhandler-kt }

The server side of `button(...)`: the `button-update` websocket command, which carries one press
or release from the browser and runs the box's callback with it.

A button is the one control in the family whose value is not worth keeping. The handler updates
the in-memory control registry so other clients see the press, broadcasts that, and calls the
callback; nothing reaches the box's saved value cache, so re-running the box does not replay the
press. Everything else about a button is in the controls DSL in `outputs.kt` and in
`sliders.js`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/server/ButtonControlHandler.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/ButtonControlHandler/)

## CustomMarking.kt { #custommarking-kt }

Custom marking menus: [`Box.customMarking`](workspace.md#custommarking-kt--custommarking) maps a direction and a label to a callback, and the frontend
shows the entries as a radial menu on the box.

[`MarkingDirections`](workspace.md#custommarking-kt-markingdirections) names the directions and their angles. When the menu is shown the server
registers each callback under an id and sends the frontend serialisable entries; choosing an
entry runs its callback.

## NetStats.kt { #netstats-kt }

Per-second counters of WebSocket traffic between the backend and the browser, shown on the pinned "net" console row.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/server/NetStats.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/NetStats/)

### NetStats { #netstats-kt-netstats }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">NetStats</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/NetStats/#L39)

Time-windowed WebSocket traffic stats for the front-end `/ws` channel, surfaced on the pinned "net" console row: `↑` = backend → front end, `↓` = front end → backend. Counters are bumped at the send choke point (`sendWithOutputBackPressure`) and the inbound frame loop; a 1s reporter emits per-second packet + KB rates — and only when there's traffic, so the pinned row dims then expires when the front end goes idle (see PinnedConsole's lifecycle).

## OscEditorBackdoor.kt { #osceditorbackdoor-kt }

Lets an OSC controller drive the editor by forwarding float, launch and stop messages to the front end as `osc-editor` commands.

[`OscEditorBackdoor`](workspace.md#osceditorbackdoor-kt-osceditorbackdoor) reads its port, addresses, debounce and delta mode from [`FieldPreferences`](workspace.md#dir-kt-fieldpreferences),
listens with an `OSCPortIn`, and forwards each matching message to the front end as an
`osc-editor` message. [`OscEditorBackdoor.learnNextAddress`](workspace.md#osceditorbackdoor-kt--osceditorbackdoor--learnnextaddress) listens once on a port and returns the
first address it hears, for filling in the preferences.

## Server.kt { #server-kt }

The Field server: the Ktor HTTPS and WebSocket application that holds open documents, runs box
code and answers the browser's RPC messages.

[`Server`](workspace.md#server-kt-server) starts the HTTPS listener (and the loopback HTTP mirror), mounts the `/ws` socket and
the static and iframe routes such as `/browse`, `/inspect` and `/logs`, and installs the message
handlers. Each connected browser has a [`SessionInformation`](workspace.md#server-kt-sessioninformation) for the document it shows;
[`sessions`](workspace.md#server-kt--sessions) maps sockets to those, and [`documents`](workspace.md#server-kt--documents) maps document names to them.
[`OutputBackPressure`](workspace.md#server-kt-outputbackpressure) limits how much box output is in flight to a client at once. Command-line
options such as `--workspace` and `--document` are read here as [`home`](workspace.md#server-kt--home) and [`documentArgument`](workspace.md#server-kt--documentargument).

### OutputBackPressureSnapshot { #server-kt-outputbackpressuresnapshot }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">OutputBackPressureSnapshot</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">pending</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">skipped</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">buffered</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxPending</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">bufferSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/Server/#L1020)

Tracks per-session back pressure for output messages. When the frontend is slow to acknowledge outputs, the pending count rises. Once it reaches [`maxPending`](workspace.md#server-kt--outputbackpressuresnapshot--maxpending), new outputs are held in a rolling buffer of size [`bufferSize`](workspace.md#server-kt--outputbackpressuresnapshot--buffersize). Messages that overflow the buffer are counted as truly skipped. When pressure eases, the buffered messages are flushed after the skip notification — they are never counted as skipped.

## StopWatch.kt { #stopwatch-kt }

Tells a box's clients when a stop has not taken effect, so the box's status marker can say
"asked to stop, not responding".

A stop is carried out on the runloop. When the runloop is blocked (a box sleeping or in a busy
loop, or a `propUp` pull of one, whose nested pump does not advance [`Runloop.frame`](workspace.md#runloop-kt--runloop--frame)), nothing
stops until the block ends, and the client's own running state can already say "stopped"
because the queued launch was cancelled. So the test is server-side: the stop is pending while
the runloop has not finished a tick since the stop was asked for, or while the box is still
inside a run. It is watched from a daemon thread, because a blocked runloop cannot report on
itself.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/server/StopWatch.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/StopWatch/)

## UserThemeManager.kt { #userthememanager-kt }

Serves the user's CSS theme from `~/.afield/theme.css` to the browser and pushes it again whenever the file changes.

[`UserThemeManager.start`](workspace.md#userthememanager-kt--userthememanager--start) creates the file with seed tokens if it is missing, then polls its
modification time and size and broadcasts the new CSS to every client on a change.
[`UserThemeManager.sendTo`](workspace.md#userthememanager-kt--userthememanager--sendto) sends the current theme to one session.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/server/UserThemeManager.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/UserThemeManager/)

## browsing.kt { #browsing-kt }

The object inspector behind `/browse`: a live, clickable tree of any value, reached from a box
with [`Inspector.linkFor`](workspace.md#browsing-kt--inspector--linkfor).

A value takes part by implementing [`Browsable`](workspace.md#browsing-kt-browsable) (a heading, a directory of named children,
optional HTML) or [`HasBrowsable`](workspace.md#browsing-kt-hasbrowsable). Other values fall back to [`BrowsableAdapters`](workspace.md#browsing-kt-browsableadapters) and to the HTML
renderers registered with [`LeafRenderers`](workspace.md#browsing-kt-leafrenderers). [`installInspectorHandler`](workspace.md#browsing-kt--installinspectorhandler) installs the socket handler
the browser's inspector page talks to.

## chat.kt { #chat-kt }

The server side of the Discussion thread that a slideshow step or a box can show: two RPC
handlers that carry messages between Field's clients and an outside chat service.

A thread is addressed by an id and a number, and the pair is a name rather than a location:
`withChat(id)` on a step can hand it a template id, so that every document made from the same
template shares one thread, and `Box.withChat` passes the box's own id. `load-chat-messages`
fetches a thread and replies only to the client that asked for it; `post-chat-message` sends one
and then broadcasts `chat-message-posted` to every client of the session, so any open widget
reloads the thread. Field's browser never calls the service itself.

Field ships no such service. The Python one was removed from the repository in October 2026, so
unless something compatible is listening on `CHAT_SERVER_URL` the Discussion UI appears, loads an
empty thread and drops what is posted into it. The rest of a slideshow is unaffected by that: the
requests run outside slideshow execution, a failed load is answered as an empty list, and a
failed post is logged and not answered at all. `dev_docs/GUIDE_CHAT_QUICKSTART.md` lists what a
replacement backend would have to serve.

## controllers.kt { #controllers-kt }

The phone controller surface: the `/controllers` routes that let a second device see and drive
the selected box's controls and outputs.

[`installControllerRoutes`](workspace.md#controllers-kt--installcontrollerroutes) mounts the controller page, a `/controllers/controls` and `/controllers/outputs`
JSON view, and the `/controllers/ws` socket, which carries control edits and touch gestures back
into Field. The `recordController...` and [`broadcastControllerControlUpdates`](workspace.md#controllers-kt--broadcastcontrollercontrolupdates) functions keep
connected controllers current as output, selection and control values change in the editor.

## docsAnnotations.kt { #docsannotations-kt }

Notes written on a documentation page, and the `/field-docs/` mirror those pages are read
through.

Three things live here. The access policy and its guards, which every docs route in Field is
checked against. The annotation notebook: the types a note is made of, the store that keeps them
in one JSON file, and the `/api/docs-annotations…` routes the panel reads and writes. And the
mirror itself, which by default serves this checkout's built site when there is one and
otherwise proxies the published site, injecting the annotation panel into each page either way.
`AFIELD_DOCS_MIRROR_SOURCE` pins it to one or the other.

### Access control

Two groups of routes are installed here, into the same Ktor application as an SSL connector that
binds `0.0.0.0` (see `Server.kt`, `httpsHost`), because Field genuinely does serve browsers and
the visionOS shell on other devices:

 - the annotation routes, `/api/docs-annotations…`. A note is not a private notepad: it is the
   prompt the revision pass hands its agents, so whoever can write one can steer a run the human
   later starts. Loopback and same-site by default, with two hatches
   (`AFIELD_DOCS_ANNOTATIONS_ALLOW_REMOTE`, `AFIELD_DOCS_ANNOTATIONS_ALLOW_CROSS_SITE`) that
   re-open them to other devices and other websites respectively;
 - the revision pass, `/api/docs-improvement/pass…` and `/docs-pass-site/…` (`docsPass.kt`),
   which runs coding agents with write access to the checkout `docsImprovementCheckout` names.
   Loopback and same-site with both hatches forced shut, so a hatch named for annotations can
   never open it.

What this does not claim to defend against is another process running as the same user on the
same machine. It can reach loopback, and in any case already has whatever access the coding
agents would be given. The boundary drawn here is this machine's own user, not this machine.

## docsPass.kt { #docspass-kt }

The documentation revision pass, as a page: `/docs-pass.html`.

Everything a pass does is `tools/docs_notes.py pass …`, and works the same from a terminal: make
a worktree, drain the notes queue with one agent per page, show the handoffs and the diff,
rebuild the docs, commit, land on `main`, remove the worktree. This file only runs those
commands for the page, one long job at a time, keeping the complete output on disk and the last
part of it in memory for the page to poll.

Every route here is loopback and same-site and nothing else: a browser on this machine, on one
of Field's own pages. The boundary is this machine's own user rather than this machine, and it
is what stops the two real attacks, another device on the network and a web page open in your
browser. There is no feature switch and no token, because a token scrolls out of the terminal it
is printed in, and the page is used from inside Field itself. What that gives up is a backstop
for a future change to the CORS or same-site code; the checks themselves are the ones
`DocsAnnotationRouteSecurityTest` pins.

Both annotation hatches are forced shut for these routes. With only two checks left,
`AFIELD_DOCS_ANNOTATIONS_ALLOW_REMOTE`, which is set for taking notes from a tablet, must not
turn out to let the tablet start agents, commit, and move `main`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/server/docsPass.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/docsPass/)

## docsSourceFile.kt { #docssourcefile-kt }

A repo source file, from this checkout, for the docs pane.

The docs build links a code span that is exactly a tracked repo path under `src/`, `tools/`,
`server/` or `public/` to GitHub (`link_repo_source_paths_html` in `public/docs_hooks.py`).
Inside Field's own docs pane that is the wrong copy: the file is on this machine, and may be
ahead of `main`. So `docsAnnotations.js`, which the `/field-docs/` mirror injects into each page,
intercepts the click and shows the file this route returns.

It is a read of source text, which is exactly the exposure `GET /api/source` has without a guard
(see `installFieldApiSameSiteGuard` in `Server.kt`). This one is guarded like the revision pass's
routes: loopback and same-site, with both annotation hatches forced shut, so it answers only a
browser on this machine, on one of Field's own pages. It serves the four roots the docs link and
nothing else: no `dev_docs/`, no `config/`, no build output, no path that leaves its root through
`..` or a symlink.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/server/docsSourceFile.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/docsSourceFile/)

## dynamicRouting.kt { #dynamicrouting-kt }

A registry that maps URI prefixes to directories, so the server can serve files from folders chosen at runtime.

The `/local` route in `Server.kt` looks up a request path in [`dynamicRoutes`](workspace.md#dynamicrouting-kt--dynamicroutes), longest matching
prefix first, and serves the file from the directory registered for that prefix.

## fileproxy.kt { #fileproxy-kt }

File proxy boxes: a box whose `contents` mirror a text file, given by an absolute path or by a
path under the workspace or the document folder.

[`refreshFileProxyBox`](workspace.md#fileproxy-kt--refreshfileproxybox) and [`refreshFileProxyBoxes`](workspace.md#fileproxy-kt--refreshfileproxyboxes) reload a proxy from disk, and
[`writeFileProxyContents`](workspace.md#fileproxy-kt--writefileproxycontents) writes an edit back, reporting the outcome as a [`FileProxyWriteResult`](workspace.md#fileproxy-kt-fileproxywriteresult).
A workspace or document proxy's path is checked to stay inside that folder; an absolute one is not. [`fileProxyHandlers`](workspace.md#fileproxy-kt--fileproxyhandlers)
installs the `create-file-proxy-box` handler the editor uses to make one.

## importing.kt { #importing-kt }

Server handlers that import boxes from a dropped `metadata.edn` or Jupyter notebook, and export Python cells back to `.ipynb`.

[`importing`](workspace.md#importing-kt--importing) installs four message handlers: `import-metadata-edn` and `import-metadata-edn-nested`

cells into boxes ([`importNotebookCells`](workspace.md#importing-kt--importnotebookcells)), and `export-ipynb` writes a Python root's cells out as a

## inspecting.kt { #inspecting-kt }

A two-way debug inspector for a box: [`Box.inspect`](workspace.md#inspecting-kt--inspect) shows a set of objects in an iframe at
`/inspect` and lets the page edit their fields.

The shape of what is shown is described by a list of [`TypeDef`](workspace.md#inspecting-kt-typedef)s. [`extractMappedData`](workspace.md#inspecting-kt--extractmappeddata) walks the
roots against those definitions and records a setter for each editable path, and
[`DebugSocketBridge`](workspace.md#inspecting-kt-debugsocketbridge) sends the extract to the page and applies the edits it sends back.
[`initInspecting`](workspace.md#inspecting-kt--initinspecting) installs the raw socket handler that routes inspector messages to the right
bridge.

## keyframeBrowsing.kt { #keyframebrowsing-kt }

The server half of the keyframe collection browser: one `/ws` raw channel, no new HTTP route.

The page itself is `keyframe_browser.html`, served by the static mount over
`src/commonMain/resources`, so nothing here widens Field's HTTP surface — which matters, because
every verbless `route(…) { handle { … } }` is an unauthenticated all-methods endpoint and there is
a census test counting them (`FieldApiCorsExposureTest`). A raw channel rides the socket the
client already has, the way the h2 explorer and the log stream do.

### What crosses the wire

Structure as JSON, presentation as HTML. The collection summary, the slot bands and the version
rows are typed payloads the page lays out itself; individual *values* come over as rendered HTML
from `.h`, which is what reusing the value visualizers buys: a `Vector3f` arrives with its axis
widget already drawn, and a type that registers its own printer gets it for free.

### Read-only

There is an `apply` op, because putting a saved look back is the reason you were browsing. There
is no edit op. Everything on disk is append-only by construction — `saveKey` never overwrites a
numbered version and an unreadable manifest is quarantined rather than replaced — and an
in-browser edit button would break that. Getting a modified look back out goes through
`updateCode`, which emits pasteable Kotlin.

## logstream.kt { #logstream-kt }

The log archive behind the `/logs` iframe: [`LogStream`](workspace.md#logstream-kt-logstream) keeps recent log records (still printing
them to stdout) and streams them to the page.

The page can ask for a filtered subset of the archive and then receive new entries live.
[`installLogStreamHandler`](workspace.md#logstream-kt--installlogstreamhandler) installs the socket handler it uses.

## terminal.kt { #terminal-kt }

A real terminal in the browser: `/terminal.html` (xterm.js) over the `/pty/<id>` WebSocket, with
a pseudo-terminal (pty4j) on this side.

Its first job is running an interactive agent (`claude` or `codex`) on one handoff batch of the
documentation revision pass, started from that batch on `/docs-pass.html` with one sentence of
direction, so the agent works through the batch's handoffs and the human answers it in place
instead of copying a command into a terminal of their own.

This hands out a process on this machine, so the boundary is the revision pass's and nothing
looser: loopback and same-site, with the annotation hatches forced shut, on every route here and
on the WebSocket upgrade. And the client never names a command or a directory: it picks one of
the [`TerminalLaunch`](workspace.md#terminal-kt-terminallaunch) kinds, and the server builds the argv and finds the directory. There is no
"run this shell line".

### Protocol on `/pty/<id>`

Server to client, binary frames are terminal output, the scrollback first on every connect so a
reload re-attaches; a text frame `{"type":"exit","code":N}` ends it. Client to server, binary or
text frames are keystrokes, except a text frame that is a JSON object with `"type":"resize"`,
which carries `cols` and `rows`. Closing the page detaches; the process keeps running until it
exits or is killed through `POST /api/terminal/<id>/kill`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/server/terminal.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/terminal/)

## upstreamcheck.kt { #upstreamcheck-kt }

Field is distributed as source: you clone it and you build it. So "is there an update" is not a
question about a version manifest and a zip, it is a question about your checkout and its remote
— and git already answers it. This asks, and reports. It never writes to the working tree; pulling
is yours to do, because only you know whether your checkout has work in it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/server/upstreamcheck.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/upstreamcheck/)

## PersonalLayer.kt { #personallayer-kt }

Loads the gitignored `src/personal` jar in its own classloader between core Field and the REPL,
so box code can use personal classes and the layer can be replaced without restarting.

[`PersonalLayer`](workspace.md#personallayer-kt-personallayer) owns the loader; `PersonalReload.kt` handles the objects an old layer leaves
behind after a reload.

## PersonalLayerSmokeTest.kt { #personallayersmoketest-kt }

Guards the [`PersonalLayer`](workspace.md#personallayer-kt-personallayer) boundary: `src/personal` is off the app `-cp` and reachable only
through its own classloader, so the ways it can quietly stop working are all invisible.

Each of these fails silently rather than loudly if it regresses — box code stops resolving
personal symbols with an ordinary "unresolved reference", which looks like a user typo; and
completion just returns fewer candidates. Hence a test rather than trust:

 1. personal really is off `-cp` (otherwise the layer is decorative and Phase 2 can never drop it),
 2. [`PersonalLayer.wrap`](workspace.md#personallayer-kt--personallayer--wrap) is idempotent (Server.main installs the layer as the context classloader,
    so KI2's `wrap(contextClassLoader)` must not stack a second layer on top of the first),
 3. and — the one that actually matters — the K2 REPL both *compiles* and *runs* against it.
    Compilation is the subtle half: it works only because
    `dependenciesFromClassloader(wholeClasspath = true)` walks the parent chain collecting each
    loader's URLs, which is behaviour of the Kotlin scripting library, not of anything here.

Skips (exit 0) when there is no `src/personal`, which is the normal state for everyone but Marc.

## PersonalReload.kt { #personalreload-kt }

Reloading [`PersonalLayer`](workspace.md#personallayer-kt-personallayer) at runtime, and coping with the objects the old one left behind.

[`reloadPersonal`](workspace.md#personalreload-kt--reloadpersonal) retires the live layer so the next engine compiles and runs against a freshly
built `afield-personal.jar`. The hard part is not the swap, it is that every already-evaluated
snippet holds classes from the layer that just died: an object made by gen-0 `kiwi.Solver` and an
object made by gen-1 `kiwi.Solver` are unrelated types, and mixing them produces the JVM's least
helpful error, `class kiwi.Solver cannot be cast to class kiwi.Solver`.

Two halves, a scan up front and a diagnosis at the point of failure:

 * [`scanForStaleClasses`](workspace.md#personalreload-kt--scanforstaleclasses) is a shallow, best-effort look at what an engine is holding, so the
   common case — a box with a personal object in a top-level `val` — gets caught and reset up
   front. It is deliberately incomplete (see its own docs) and makes no attempt to be otherwise.
 * [`staleLayerDiagnosis`](workspace.md#personalreload-kt--stalelayerdiagnosis) catches what the scan missed, at the moment it actually breaks, and says
   so in English. Because recovery is a one-click reset rather than a debugging session, the scan
   does not have to be good — it only has to keep most boxes from visibly hiccuping.

Neither half re-runs anything. A box whose engine was recycled is *marked* ([`needsRerun`](workspace.md#personalreload-kt--needsrerun)) and left
alone: Field does not execute user code that the user did not ask to execute, and a reload is not
an exception to that — re-running a box can open windows, start strands and hit the network.

## util_settings.kt { #util-settings-kt }

Property delegates that keep a single `String`, `Int` or `Double` value across Field restarts,
one small file per property name under `.field/` in the working directory.

Declare a property `by PersistentString { "default" }` (or [`PersistentInt`](workspace.md#util-settings-kt-persistentint), [`PersistentDouble`](workspace.md#util-settings-kt-persistentdouble)).
The first read loads `.field/<propertyName>` through [`PersistOnExit.load`](workspace.md#util-settings-kt--persistonexit--load) and falls back to the
default when the file is missing; a write records the value in
[`PersistOnExit.needingPersistance`](workspace.md#util-settings-kt--persistonexit--needingpersistance). A daemon thread writes pending values about once a second,
and a shutdown hook writes whatever is left on a graceful exit.

The file is named by the Kotlin property name alone, so two persistent properties with the same
name share one file.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/settings/util_settings.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/settings/util_settings/)

## stdlib_collections.kt { #stdlib-collections-kt }

Loop, collection and string shorthands, and the truthiness test for a raw property value.

`10 { i -> ... }` and `(0..9) { i -> ... }` call a block once per index and collect the results,
and `20 alphas { a -> ... }` does the same over evenly spaced values from 0.0 to 1.0 inclusive,
which is the loop that parameterises a curve so that it closes. The rest are conversions and
slices: `list[2..5]` for an inclusive copy, `List.m` and `List.s` for a mutable copy and a set,
`String.r` for a compiled `Regex`, `"ab" * 3` for repetition. `isTrue` reads an `Any?` as a yes
or a no, and is true only for `true`, a non-zero `Int` and a non-empty `String`.

One of the `stdlib` files, which the `intro` preamble star-imports into every box, so everything
here can be called unqualified, with `Box` as the implicit receiver.

## ContextResolution.kt { #contextresolution-kt }

The graph walk that decides which box supplies a value read through `fromContext`, `prop` or `@exported`.

Every lookup starts at the asking box and moves up through its ancestors one generation at a time;
the nearest match wins. A [`ContextResolution.Query`](workspace.md#contextresolution-kt--contextresolution--query) says what counts as a match and a
[`ContextResolution.Policy`](workspace.md#contextresolution-kt--contextresolution--policy) says which parts of each box are searched, and in what order.
[`ContextResolution.explain`](workspace.md#contextresolution-kt--contextresolution--explain) runs the same walk to the end of the graph and reports the winner,
the path to it, and anything it shadowed, as a [`WhyAnswer`](workspace.md#whyanswer-kt-whyanswer).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/document/context/ContextResolution.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/document/context/ContextResolution/)

## ContextWhy.kt { #contextwhy-kt }

Builds the JSON answer to "why did this value resolve here?" for the backdoor, MCP and AI tools.

[`ContextWhy.explain`](workspace.md#contextwhy-kt--contextwhy--explain) takes a box and a name or a type. The answer names the supplying box, the path of
parents to it, whether the value was a property or a live variable, and what it shadows. For a
name declared in the box's preamble it also names that preamble line and the box it came from.

## ContextWhyTools.kt { #contextwhytools-kt }

The AI tool `WhyDoesThisResolve`, which lets the in-app assistant ask where a box's value comes from.

It takes a name or a type and, optionally, a box (the focused one by default), and returns the
same explanation as [`ContextResolution.explain`](workspace.md#contextresolution-kt--contextresolution--explain). [`installContextWhyTools`](workspace.md#contextwhytools-kt--installcontextwhytools)
registers it.

## WhyAnswer.kt { #whyanswer-kt }

The value a box gets back when it asks where one of its inputs comes from.

[`ContextResolution.explain`](workspace.md#contextresolution-kt--contextresolution--explain) and `why.<name>` both return a [`WhyAnswer`](workspace.md#whyanswer-kt-whyanswer). Printing it gives a
one-sentence summary, `.h` shows it as a card, and `.h2` lays out its fields to explore. The full
JSON answer stays available as `WhyAnswer.json`.

## why.kt { #why-kt }

`why.speed`, a completable way to ask where a box's `prop`-declared value comes from.

Every `prop<T>(name)` also declares `name` on [`Why`](workspace.md#why-kt-why), so typing `why.` in a box lists the names it
inherits; each one returns a [`WhyAnswer`](workspace.md#whyanswer-kt-whyanswer). For any other name, or to ask by type, call
[`ContextResolution.explain`](workspace.md#contextresolution-kt--contextresolution--explain) directly.

## Boxes.kt { #boxes-kt }

The [`Box`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-box) model: a box's properties, its `children`/`parents` graph, and the property sets that
decide what is saved and what is sent to the browser.

[`Box`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-box) holds its properties in a property bag and implements [`HasProperties`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-hasproperties) and [`HasHierarchy`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-hashierarchy).
[`Box.connect`](workspace.md#boxes-kt--box--connect) and [`Box.disconnect`](workspace.md#boxes-kt--box--disconnect) edit the edge sets (`children` by default). The companion's
`ioPersistentProperties` lists what is written to `metadata.edn`, `ioSeparateProperties` maps the
properties written as sidecar files to their extensions (`code` to `kt`, shader stages to `glsl`),
and `uiResyncProperties` lists what is pushed to connected clients when it changes.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/document/graph/Boxes.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/document/graph/Boxes/)

## nesting.kt { #nesting-kt }

Nesting: drawing one box inside another, through the `nested` and `nestedIn` properties.

A nested box is also connected to its container, so it inherits the container's imports and
marked preamble lines. Setting [`nested`](workspace.md#nesting-kt--nested) or [`nestedIn`](workspace.md#nesting-kt--nestedin) keeps both sides and the edge in step;
[`nestInto`](workspace.md#nesting-kt--nestinto) also converts the frame to and from parent-relative coordinates, and refuses a cycle.
[`reconcileNestingEdges`](workspace.md#nesting-kt--reconcilenestingedges) re-derives missing edges for boxes loaded from disk. The behaviour is
covered by `NestingConnectsTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/document/graph/nesting.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/document/graph/nesting/)

## stdlib_graph.kt { #stdlib-graph-kt }

Finding boxes by name, connecting them, and hanging scratch state off one.

`named` is how one box gets hold of another, searching the whole document from the root and
skipping the tombstoned boxes a delete leaves behind. `parent += child` and `parent -= child`
connect and disconnect, and connection is the edge property inheritance walks. [`Marker`](workspace.md#stdlib-graph-kt-marker) is a
named property bag attached to a box, obtained with `__m` and created on first use, for state
that belongs to part of a box rather than to the box itself; it lives in memory only and is not
saved with the document.

One of the `stdlib` files, which the `intro` preamble star-imports into every box, so everything
here can be called unqualified, with `Box` as the implicit receiver.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/document/graph/stdlib_graph.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/document/graph/stdlib_graph/)

## HistoryMetrics.kt { #historymetrics-kt }

Per-version activity and screenshot records for a document, stored in its
`history_metrics.edn` beside `metadata.edn`.

Each record is keyed by version index. A save adds the activity the flight recorder saw since the
previous save (per-box counts included), a diff adds its edit statistics, and a captured
screenshot adds a reference to its image file. The history browser reads these back through
[`HistoryMetrics.activityByVersion`](workspace.md#historymetrics-kt--historymetrics--activitybyversion) to annotate its timeline.

## history.kt { #history-kt }

A document's version history on disk: listing, diffing, searching, naming and restoring the
saved versions under its `backups/` folder, plus the RPC handlers behind the history browser.

[`HistoryManager`](workspace.md#history-kt-historymanager) owns the version list and every operation on it; [`installHistoryHandlers`](workspace.md#history-kt--installhistoryhandlers)
registers the messages `history.html` sends (`list-history-versions`,
`diff-history-version`, `restore-history-version` and the rest). Per-version activity and
screenshot records live alongside in [`HistoryMetrics`](workspace.md#historymetrics-kt-historymetrics).

## FileWatchManager.kt { #filewatchmanager-kt }

Reloads an open document's properties when their sidecar files are edited outside Field.

A [`FileWatchManager`](workspace.md#filewatchmanager-kt-filewatchmanager) watches one document folder and tells Field's own saves apart from external
edits by content hash, so editing a box's `.kt` or `.glsl` sidecar in another editor updates the box
in the running session.

## LinalgSerialization.kt { #linalgserialization-kt }

JSON serializers for Field's vector and quaternion types, and the [`FieldJson`](workspace.md#linalgserialization-kt--fieldjson) instance that uses them.

Each serializer writes its value as a flat JSON array of floats (two, three or four for the vectors,
four for `Quaternionf`, eight for [`DualQuaternionf`](math.md#dualquaternionf-kt-dualquaternionf)) and rejects an array of the wrong length on the
way back. [`FieldSerializersModule`](workspace.md#linalgserialization-kt--fieldserializersmodule) registers them as contextual serializers.

## PersistedFingerprint.kt { #persistedfingerprint-kt }

The content hash that catches a document edit dirty marking did not see.

Field decides whether to save by marking: a write through `setPropertyRaw`, `removePropertyRaw`,
`connect` or `disconnect` tells the session there is something to write. A collection mutated in
place and a write made while the document is still loading go through none of them. So the
autosave tick, the detach save and the shutdown flush also hash what they would write and compare
that against the hash from the last time the document matched disk, saving when the two differ.

The per-property entries behind the hash are kept as well, which lets a tripwire name the
`(box id, property)` pairs that changed without being marked. Each one names a mutator that
should have marked its own write.

## SafeSaveAtomicSmokeTest.kt { #safesaveatomicsmoketest-kt }

Smoke for [`File.safeSave`](workspace.md#saving-kt--safesave)'s `atomic = true` path, which is what keeps a file readable while it is
being rewritten. The operation-transcript writer (`OperationTranscript.checkpoint` and friends)
uses it for `operations.yaml`: the text goes to a temp file in the same directory and is then
renamed into place, so a concurrent reader — another thread, or another process sharing the
workspace — only ever sees a complete file.

`concurrentAtomicWritesNeverTear` is the case that exercises that. Six writer threads replace one
file 120 times each, with payloads of very different lengths, while a reader parses it in
a tight loop. A torn or interleaved write splices one payload into another and SnakeYAML reports
`expected <block end>`; under atomic writes every read parses to a list.

## edn.kt { #edn-kt }

An EDN reader and printer, the text format of a document's `metadata.edn`.

[`Edn.read`](workspace.md#edn-kt--edn--read) and [`Edn.write`](workspace.md#edn-kt--edn--write) convert between EDN text and plain Kotlin values (maps, lists, strings,
numbers), and [`EdnValue`](workspace.md#edn-kt-ednvalue) is the parsed tree in between. Tagged values such as `#afield/rect` are
handled by registering a type with [`Edn.CustomTypes`](workspace.md#edn-kt--edn--customtypes).

## saving.kt { #saving-kt }

Reads and writes a document as `metadata.edn` plus sidecar files, and keeps backups of what it replaces.

[`SavingContext`](workspace.md#saving-kt-savingcontext) is the canonical reader and writer of the version 2 document format: it saves a set
of boxes to `metadata.edn`, writing large text properties such as `code` or `fragment` to
`<uid>_<property>_.<ext>` sidecars, and loads a document folder (or EDN text) back into boxes.
[`File.safeSave`](workspace.md#saving-kt--safesave) is the file write underneath it, which keeps the previous version in a `backups/`
directory and can write atomically through a temp file and a rename.

## PropertyBag.kt { #propertybag-kt }

The thread-safe, insertion-ordered map that holds every [`Box`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-box)'s properties.

[`PropertyBag`](workspace.md#propertybag-kt-propertybag) below explains the guarantees: single-key operations are serialised, and `keys`,
`values` and `entries` iterate snapshots that write removals through to the live map. The view
behaviour is pinned by `PropertyBagViewTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/document/properties/PropertyBag.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/document/properties/PropertyBag/)

The property bag behind every [`Box`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-box) — an insertion-ordered, null-tolerant map that is safe to read, write **and iterate** from more than one thread at once.

## PropertyDependencies.kt { #propertydependencies-kt }

Records which boxes read values held by other boxes, per document, and saves that record as
`dependencies.edn` beside `metadata.edn`.

[`PropertyDependencies`](workspace.md#propertydependencies-kt-propertydependencies) below describes what is recorded and when it is written; the tests are
`PropertyDependenciesTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/document/properties/PropertyDependencies.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/document/properties/PropertyDependencies/)

## props.kt { #props-kt }

The `prop` / `rootProp` macro pair — the typed, inheritable box-property slot.

[`prop`](workspace.md#props-kt--prop) and [`rootProp`](workspace.md#props-kt--rootprop) exist only as the declarations that make `prop<Int>(foo)` resolve; neither
is meant to run, and calling one throws `MacroRegistry.MacroNotExpandedException`. The real work
happens at expansion time in [`macro_prop`](workspace.md#props-kt--macro-prop) and [`macro_root_prop`](workspace.md#props-kt--macro-root-prop), which are handed the type
argument and the name, and return an `Insert` that rewrites the call site to the bare name (or
`root.name`) and pushes two declarations into the box's preamble: a
`var Box.<name> by Inheritance<T>()`, a `val Once.<name> by Onceing<T>()` and a
`val Why.<name> by Whying()` (so `why.<name>` explains where the value comes from). All three generated
lines carry the trailing empty-comment marker that makes the preamble gather copy them down into
child boxes, and an import for `T` is added via `kotlinImportStatementFor`. [`macro_root_prop`](workspace.md#props-kt--macro-root-prop)
differs only in targeting `this.root`, so the accessors land on the document root rather than
on the calling box.

## reactiveProps.kt { #reactiveprops-kt }

`propUp`, `propDown` and `propUpDown`: [`prop`](workspace.md#props-kt--prop) with re-execution attached.

All three declare the same typed, inherited slot `prop` does (a `var Box.<name>` in the preamble,
copied down into children), and read and write it the same way. What they add:

- **Up** — a read that finds no value anywhere up the graph runs the box that supplies it, then
  reads again. The supplier is the box that declared the property (or supplied it before), nearest
  first, and the run happens *inside* the read, so a chain of them unwinds in order.
- **Down** — a write that changes the value reruns, after the writing box's run has finished,
  every box that read the old value, in dependency order.

Declare it where the value is written (Down is decided by the writer's declaration, Up by the
reader's), and the declaration reaches the children as `prop`'s does. The scheduling is
`afield.runtime.lifecycle.ReactiveRuns`; what it did is in `ReactiveRuns.recentEvents()`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/document/properties/reactiveProps.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/document/properties/reactiveProps/)

## stdlib_properties.kt { #stdlib-properties-kt }

The property delegates that `prop` and `@exported` generate against.

[`Delegation`](workspace.md#stdlib-properties-kt-delegation) stores a value in the receiver's own property bag rather than in a Kotlin field,
which is what makes such a property survive a re-run and show up in the property inspector.
[`Inheritance`](workspace.md#stdlib-properties-kt-inheritance) walks up `parents` until some ancestor has the property, throwing
[`MissingInheritedPropertyException`](workspace.md#stdlib-properties-kt-missinginheritedpropertyexception) with a message naming the property and the box when nothing
does; [`InheritanceFromContext`](workspace.md#stdlib-properties-kt-inheritancefromcontext) makes the same walk but prefers each box's live Kotlin variables
over raw properties. [`inheritedPropertyRaw`](workspace.md#stdlib-properties-kt--inheritedpropertyraw) is that lookup without a `KProperty` to perform it
through, for readers such as FieldML that have no generated delegate to read it with.

One of the `stdlib` files, which the `intro` preamble star-imports into every box, so everything
here can be called unqualified, with `Box` as the implicit receiver.

## KitDedicatedHost.kt { #kitdedicatedhost-kt }

The compatibility route for a project that already has its own launcher, workspace and document
conventions and wants to appear in Welcome's kit library without adopting Field's. Such a kit
declares a `host` block in its `field-kit.json` naming a launcher script, a loopback HTTP endpoint
and the workspace that launcher owns, and Field then treats it as something to start rather than
something to load: none of its runtime declarations join the calling host's classpath, and its
documents keep whatever versioning scheme the project already uses.

[`KitDedicatedHosts.open`](workspace.md#kitdedicatedhost-kt--kitdedicatedhosts--open) is the whole action, and it runs only from an explicit **Open kit host**
or **Create in kit host** in Welcome, never from adding a kit. It probes `/api/instance-info` at
the declared endpoint first and reuses a host that is already up, refusing outright when a
different workspace answers there; otherwise it runs the launcher from the kit's source directory
with Field's own port and path variables stripped from the environment, appends its output to
`logs/<id>.log` under the kits directory, and polls for up to three minutes. Creating a document
is then a POST to that host's own starting-point API, so the running project copies the seed by
its own rules and hands back the URL to open.

Two checks hold the arrangement together. [`KitPackages.read`](workspace.md#kitpackages-kt--kitpackages--read) calls [`KitDedicatedHosts.validate`](workspace.md#kitdedicatedhost-kt--kitdedicatedhosts--validate) on
every manifest, so a non-loopback endpoint, a query string, user info in the URL, or a launcher
path escaping the package is refused when the kit is added rather than when it is run. And
[`KitDedicatedHosts.open`](workspace.md#kitdedicatedhost-kt--kitdedicatedhosts--open) compares the launcher's hash in the source directory against the one in
the installed snapshot, so the script that executes is the script that was there when the kit was
added.

## KitFirstOpen.kt { #kitfirstopen-kt }

A document copied from a kit's starting point runs its roles, in the kit's launch order, the first time
it opens, so it does something without `field_kit.py activate`.

[`openStartingPointIntoWorkspace`](workspace.md#dir-kt--openstartingpointintoworkspace) leaves [`MARKER`](workspace.md#kitfirstopen-kt--kitfirstopen--marker) in a copy that holds a kit record; the server's
document-ready hook (`afield.app.server.installKitFirstOpen`) calls [`rolesToLaunch`](workspace.md#kitfirstopen-kt--kitfirstopen--rolestolaunch) and launches what it
returns, once: the marker is consumed whether or not a launch succeeds, so a role that fails is not
relaunched on every open. Later opens run only what `autorun` asks for, as for any document.

## KitInstances.kt { #kitinstances-kt }

A document copied from a kit's starting point, the record of what it received, and the three-way
comparison that updates it. [`KitInstances.create`](workspace.md#kitinstances-kt--kitinstances--create) copies a starting point into the workspace,
puts the new document in a `kit-<id>` workspace project, and writes `.field-kit-instance.json`:
the kit id, the package and runtime revisions, the starting point, the project, and a hash of
every file the copy began from. Those hashes are the baseline; the document's files are its own
from then on.

[`KitInstances.inspect`](workspace.md#kitinstances-kt--kitinstances--inspect) reads three hashes for each path (the baseline, the document's file now,
and the same path in the installed starting point) and labels the difference `update`,
`edited-here`, `remove` or `conflict`, a conflict being both sides changed since the baseline.
[`KitInstances.migrate`](workspace.md#kitinstances-kt--kitinstances--migrate) then applies that plan or none of it. It refuses outright while any path
conflicts, copies every file it is about to write or delete into `backups/kit-<uuid>` first,
restores from those copies if a write fails partway, and rewrites the record last, so a failed
update leaves the document on the revision it already had.

A document reads shared resources from the package revision it recorded rather than the newest
installed one ([`KitInstances.sharedResources`](workspace.md#kitinstances-kt--kitinstances--sharedresources)), which is also why `.field-kit-instance.json` has
to travel with the document's other files: without it a host has no kit to compare the document
against, and it opens as an ordinary workspace document. The equivalent for a role kit inside a
single document is [`Kits`](workspace.md#kits-kt-kits).

## KitPackages.kt { #kitpackages-kt }

The registry of kit packages installed on this machine, and the immutable snapshot each
registration copies out of a package's source folder. A kit package is a directory holding a
`field-kit.json` that names one or more starting points, each of them an ordinary saved Field
document, beside optional Kotlin sources, JARs, pinned Maven coordinates, native libraries and a
lifecycle class. `public/docs/kits.md` is the user's page. The smaller role-kit model, which
describes shared box code and assets inside one document, is [`Kits`](workspace.md#kits-kt-kits).

[`KitPackages.read`](workspace.md#kitpackages-kt--kitpackages--read) validates a manifest and [`KitPackages.install`](workspace.md#kitpackages-kt--kitpackages--install) copies the package to
`packages/<id>/<revision>/` under `~/.afield/kits` (`afield.kits.dir` or `AFIELD_KITS_DIR` moves
that root). The revision is a SHA-256 over the path and content hash of every declared file, so
registering unchanged source resolves to the snapshot that already exists, and a document goes on
reading the revision it recorded after a newer one arrives. Installation reads JSON and copies
bytes; it runs nothing the package ships.

Two files carry the registry to the next start of Field. `registry.json` lists the
[`InstalledKit`](workspace.md#kitpackages-kt-installedkit) snapshots, and `runtime.properties` is a launch profile that `build.gradle.kts`
reads to assemble the extension classpath, resolve the pinned dependencies, extend
`java.library.path` and pass `-Dafield.kit.packages` and `-Dafield.kit.revisions` to the host,
which is where [`KitRuntime`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt-kitruntime) picks the same set up again. A kit registered inside a running host
therefore reports `restart-required` from [`KitPackages.statuses`](workspace.md#kitpackages-kt--kitpackages--statuses) until its revision turns up in
[`KitPackages.active`](workspace.md#kitpackages-kt--kitpackages--active); those statuses are what Welcome's **Kits** area lists.

[`KitPackages.child`](workspace.md#kitpackages-kt--kitpackages--child) is the containment rule every path here goes through: package-relative, no
`..`, and canonicalised, so neither a path nor a symlink inside the package can reach a file
outside it. Because one host loads every installed runtime together, installing also refuses a
set of kits that disagree about a dependency's version, about the value of a runtime system
property, or about the contents of two native libraries with the same filename.

## KitRestarts.kt { #kitrestarts-kt }

Builds the classpath a kit needs before stopping the Field that asked for it, so a build that
fails leaves Welcome running and able to say why. Adding a kit package registers a snapshot but
loads nothing: its Kotlin extensions, pinned dependencies and native libraries reach a host only
through the launch profile [`KitPackages`](workspace.md#kitpackages-kt-kitpackages) writes, which is why **Restart Field** in Welcome's kit
area has to compile and resolve before the restart rather than after it.

[`KitRestarts.prepare`](workspace.md#kitrestarts-kt--kitrestarts--prepare) checks that this installation has both a launcher (`field.sh`, or
`field.ps1` on Windows) and a Gradle wrapper, then runs `gradlew jvmJar dumpFieldLaunch
-PfieldServerOnly=true` on a daemon thread, adding `--offline` when `AFIELD_OFFLINE` is set and
appending to `logs/restart.log` under the kits directory. The current host keeps serving
throughout. A non-zero exit, or a build still going after twenty minutes, leaves
[`KitRestarts.status`](workspace.md#kitrestarts-kt--kitrestarts--status) at phase `failed` with the message and the log path and no restart happens;
only a clean build invokes the `ready` callback, which flushes pending document saves, stops the
server and relaunches the launcher with `--server-only`. Welcome polls
`GET /api/kits/restart-status` while the build runs, and the Electron or browser window it polled
from reconnects to the new host once the restart completes.

## KitRuntime.kt { #kitruntime-kt }

Loads each installed kit runtime once per host, then attaches and detaches documents against it.
[`KitRuntime.start`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt--kitruntime--start) reads the package directories the launcher captured in `afield.kit.packages`,
instantiates each manifest's `runtime.lifecycle` class from the personal class layer and calls
[`KitLifecycle.startup`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt--kitlifecycle--startup). A kit whose startup throws is cleaned up, recorded in [`KitRuntime.errors`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt--kitruntime--errors)
and shown as an error in Welcome rather than failing the host. Opening a document that carries a
[`KitInstanceRecord`](workspace.md#kitinstances-kt-kitinstancerecord) calls [`KitRuntime.activate`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt--kitruntime--activate), which resolves the document's
[`WorkspaceProjectScope`](workspace.md#workspaceprojectscope-kt-workspaceprojectscope) and runs [`KitLifecycle.activate`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt--kitlifecycle--activate) inside its root box context; tearing that
session down calls [`KitLifecycle.deactivate`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt--kitlifecycle--deactivate).

Those package directories come from the profile Gradle read at launch, not from the registry as it
stands now, so a kit installed or updated since this host started is invisible here until a
restart.
[`KitRuntime.activate`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt--kitruntime--activate) enforces the matching condition directly: a document records the runtime
revision it was created against, and activation refuses when this host loaded a different one,
naming both.

[`KitRuntime.launchBoxes`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt--kitruntime--launchboxes) answers what a starting point asks Field to run. It reads `launch` from
the revision the *document* recorded rather than from the newer compatible one this host may
hold, so a kit that has since renamed or reordered its boxes cannot change what an existing
document launches, and it insists on exactly one live box per name instead of guessing. A
shutdown hook deactivates every live document and calls [`KitLifecycle.cleanup`](workspace.md#kitruntime-kt--kitlifecycle--cleanup) in reverse load
order, with four seconds to finish.

## Kits.kt { #kits-kt }

Kits package the shared parts of one kind of document so many documents can be installed from, and
migrated to, the same source. A kit is what every document of one kind receives: the code of the boxes that play its roles
(providers), the sources those boxes hold in other properties (a rule set, a recipe), and the
asset files they read from the document's `files/` folder. It is a directory with a `kit.json`
beside those files; `tools/field_kit.py` makes one from a document, rehashes it, installs it in
a document, migrates a document to a newer revision and publishes it as a Welcome starting point.
`public/docs/kits.md` is the user's page.

```diffstatic {data-lang=json}
{
  "schema": "field.kit.v1", "name": "rooms", "roleProperty": "kitRole",
  "launchOrder": ["rules", "plan"],
  "roles": {"rules": {"name": "Rules", "properties": {
      "code":       {"file": "roles/rules/code.kt",       "sha256": "…"},
      "roomRules":  {"file": "roles/rules/roomRules.json", "sha256": "…"},
      "rulesAudit": {"file": "roles/rules/roomRules.json", "sha256": "…", "frozen": true}}}},
  "assets": {"palette.json": "…"},
  "revision": "…"
}
```

A box plays a role when its `KitManifest.roleProperty` holds the role's key. Each property is
installed from `file` in the kit, and `sha256` is the hash of that file's bytes, which is also
the hash of the property's text (`SourceStudy.hash`). An asset `palette.json` comes from the
kit's `files/palette.json` and lands in the document's `files/palette.json`. The revision is the
hash of everything else, so two kits with the same revision install the same bytes.

**The document owns a copy.** A document on a kit records the manifest it was last installed from in `files/kit.json` (its
*record*), with the kit's directory. Nothing changes a document's copy behind its back: a newer
kit is only a difference [`Kits.inspect`](workspace.md#kits-kt--kits--inspect) reports, until a migration installs it. [`Kits.inspect`](workspace.md#kits-kt--kits--inspect) compares
three hashes for every property and asset: the record's, the document's, and the kit's.
The document matching the kit is current; matching the record (and not the kit) means the kit
changed it, which a migration installs; matching neither means the document's own edit, which
a migration refuses to overwrite. A *frozen* property is a copy the document must not edit,
such as the baseline an audit checks candidates against; a migration replaces it whenever it
differs from the kit, and says so.

## VirtualFileSystem.kt { #virtualfilesystem-kt }

A read-only view of box text in saved documents as addressable files, so tools that expect files can read
a box's code or shaders without opening Field. [`AfieldVirtualFileSystem`](workspace.md#virtualfilesystem-kt-afieldvirtualfilesystem) names each text property
`afield://<document>/<uid>/<property>`, lists them from a workspace directory (an `afield:` URI whose path
is that directory) and reads them back from `metadata.edn` or `metadata.json`, resolving sidecar files
and skipping tombstoned boxes.

Only properties in `AfieldVirtualFileSystem.DEFAULT_PROPERTIES` are exposed by default: `code` and the
GLSL and Slang shader stages, each with a language label. [`collectVirtualFiles`](workspace.md#virtualfilesystem-kt--collectvirtualfiles) combines listing roots
and reading explicit URIs across several [`VirtualFileSystem`](workspace.md#virtualfilesystem-kt-virtualfilesystem)s, dispatched by URI scheme; the AI4
filestore CLI in `afield.ai.knowledge` uses it to upload document text.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/document/workspace/VirtualFileSystem.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/document/workspace/VirtualFileSystem/)

## WorkspaceProjectScope.kt { #workspaceprojectscope-kt }

The shared box and the persistent preferences a workspace project gives every document in it. The
folder side of a project lives in `dir.kt`: a directory under the workspace's `_projects/` with a
`contents.edn` membership list, a `preferences.json` and a `files/` folder, listed by
`listWorkspaceProjects`. This file is the part of it that is live in a running host. Each
[`WorkspaceProjectScope`](workspace.md#workspaceprojectscope-kt-workspaceprojectscope) owns an invisible [`Box`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-box) whose id is `project:` followed by a hash of the
project directory, and `attachRootToMetaroot` parents a document's root box beneath the scopes it
belongs to instead of directly beneath the global metaroot. A property set on that box is
therefore inherited by every box in every document of the project, which is how a kit shares
settings and runtime objects between its documents.

From box code `projectScopes()` is the way in: `projectScopes().single().setPreference("theme",
"dark")` writes a preference that outlives the host, and [`WorkspaceProjectScope.preferences`](workspace.md#workspaceprojectscope-kt--workspaceprojectscope--preferences)
reads a snapshot of them back. A project box never reaches a document's `metadata.edn`, because
persistence filters it and the metaroot out of the saved `parents` and `children`. A document
whose project is absent attaches to the metaroot instead, with nothing dangling in its saved
graph.

[`WorkspaceProjectScopes`](workspace.md#workspaceprojectscope-kt-workspaceprojectscopes) keeps one scope per project directory for the life of the host, so two
documents in one project see the same box identity rather than two copies of it. Documents
created by [`KitInstances.create`](workspace.md#kitinstances-kt--kitinstances--create) land in a `kit-<id>` project and ordinarily have exactly one
scope, but nothing stops a document from belonging to several.

## copy.kt { #copy-kt }

Duplicating boxes inside a document: [`copyBox`](workspace.md#copy-kt--copybox) clones one box, [`copyBoxes`](workspace.md#copy-kt--copyboxes) clones a selection and
rewires its connections, and [`nextCopyName`](workspace.md#copy-kt--nextcopyname) names the results.

[`copyBox`](workspace.md#copy-kt--copybox) copies the persistent properties except the graph edges (`parents`, `children`, `nested`,
`nestedIn`), gives the copy a fresh uuid, a `(copy)` or `(copy n)` name and its own engine, connects it
under root, and by default offsets its frame by 80 in x and y. [`copyBoxes`](workspace.md#copy-kt--copyboxes) also takes every box nested
inside the selection and skips tombstoned ones. Connections between copied boxes point at the copies;
connections to boxes outside the selection are kept, so a copy stays wired to the same outside parents and
children. Only the top-level boxes of the selection are offset, so nested copies keep their place inside
their copied container.

## dir.kt { #dir-kt }

The server side of the workspace browser: listing, searching, tagging and copying the documents
under a workspace folder.

[`simpleDir`](workspace.md#dir-kt--simpledir) and [`welcomeDir`](workspace.md#dir-kt--welcomedir) list documents for the file browser and the welcome page,
[`startingPoints`](workspace.md#dir-kt--startingpoints) and [`templateStartingPoints`](workspace.md#dir-kt--templatestartingpoints) list the transcripts and templates a new document
can start from, and [`openStartingPointIntoWorkspace`](workspace.md#dir-kt--openstartingpointintoworkspace) and [`duplicateWorkspaceDocument`](workspace.md#dir-kt--duplicateworkspacedocument) copy one
into the workspace. [`searchWorkspace`](workspace.md#dir-kt--searchworkspace) searches document contents, [`updateDocumentTags`](workspace.md#dir-kt--updatedocumenttags) and
[`exportTaggedDocumentsZip`](workspace.md#dir-kt--exporttaggeddocumentszip) manage tags, and [`createWorkspaceProject`](workspace.md#dir-kt--createworkspaceproject) and its neighbours group
documents into projects stored under the workspace's `_projects` folder.

## metadata.kt { #metadata-kt }

Per-box YAML metadata and the tags read from it. A box's `metadata` property holds YAML text, saved
as the `<uid>_metadata_.yaml` sidecar; [`tagsForBox`](workspace.md#metadata-kt--tagsforbox) reads one key of it as a list of strings, and
[`tagDatabase`](workspace.md#metadata-kt--tagdatabase) scans every document folder under a workspace root for those sidecars and collects
each box's `tags`.

[`tagsForBox`](workspace.md#metadata-kt--tagsforbox) returns null when the YAML is not a map or lacks the key; [`tagDatabase`](workspace.md#metadata-kt--tagdatabase) skips a sidecar
whose YAML is not a map. A YAML syntax error is not caught in either and propagates.

## provisional.kt { #provisional-kt }

Provisional edits: proposed text for a box property, typically from AI4, held per document until someone
accepts or rejects it. Entries are kept in memory, keyed by document, box uid and property, and every
change to the entries sends the document's whole `ProvisionalSet` to its browsers as `set-provisional`.

[`acceptProvisional`](workspace.md#provisional-kt--acceptprovisional) writes the proposed text into the box, records the acceptance (with any
[`AiProvisionalArchive`](workspace.md#provisional-kt-aiprovisionalarchive) markdown attached by [`setProvisionalArchive`](workspace.md#provisional-kt--setprovisionalarchive)) in the flight recorder, and drops the
entry; [`rejectProvisional`](workspace.md#provisional-kt--rejectprovisional) only drops it. [`acceptAllProvisional`](workspace.md#provisional-kt--acceptallprovisional) and [`rejectAllProvisional`](workspace.md#provisional-kt--rejectallprovisional) do the same for
a whole document. When the decided property is a shader source (GLSL, Slang or `stackSL`) and the box already has the
matching live shader module, that module is rebuilt afterwards, once per box and shader kind, on the
runloop; rejecting reloads it too.

## stdlib_buffers.kt { #stdlib-buffers-kt }

`add` for `FloatBuffer` and `IntBuffer`: append components at the current position and return
the buffer, so writes chain.

The vertex-writing idiom, `buf.add(x, y).add(x2, y2)`. There are fixed-arity overloads for two
and three floats and for a [`Vec2`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec2), [`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3) or [`Vec4`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec4), and a vararg one that converts any
`Number`, which boxes each argument and is therefore the wrong one for a per-frame loop over
thousands of vertices. `IntBuffer.add` is the index-buffer counterpart, truncating rather than
rounding; it is called `add` because `IntBuffer.put(index, data)` already means writing at an
absolute index.

One of the `stdlib` files, which the `intro` preamble star-imports into every box, so everything
here can be called unqualified, with `Box` as the implicit receiver.

## stdlib_remotejs.kt { #stdlib-remotejs-kt }

Running JavaScript in the browser from inside a box.

`inBrowser` evaluates a string as JavaScript in every browser session attached to this
workspace, in the context of the calling box. It is fire-and-forget: nothing comes back and
there is no error channel, so a mistake in the code fails silently in the browser console. It is
the way to reach the box's own DOM, or something on the page Kotlin has no handle on.

One of the `stdlib` files, which the `intro` preamble star-imports into every box, so everything
here can be called unqualified, with `Box` as the implicit receiver.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/remotejs/stdlib_remotejs.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/remotejs/stdlib_remotejs/)
